title: The Autonomous Weapons Debate (Still) Has a Definition Problem | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Horowitz and Kahn argue the autonomous weapons debate is muddled by loose terminology and propose classifying weapons by target selection, engagement and human supervision into five types, noting autonomy has existed for decades and that real battlefield autonomy runs on simple software, not LLMs.

insights.claim: There is no consensus on what counts as an autonomous weapon: terms like killer robots, AWS and LAWS are used interchangeably for anything from a GPS-denied cruise missile to a Terminator-style system.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Policy built on vague terms may miss real risks or ban existing systems.
insights.quote: Semantic drift has produced a persistent, pernicious 180-degree problem.

insights.claim: The Pentagon-Anthropic rupture this year turned in part on the gap between Dario Amodei's definition of fully autonomous weapons and the Pentagon's term autonomous weapon systems.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Definitions are shaping AI-lab and defense-customer relations.
insights.locator: This year’s public rupture between the Pentagon

insights.claim: Autonomy is a spectrum, not a binary, defined by the technology and the human choices in employing a weapon, so the right question is how autonomous a system is.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for assessing defense-tech claims.
insights.quote: The question isn’t, “Is it autonomous?” but rather, “How autonomous is it?”
insights.locator: A central tension is that everyone wants autonomy

themes.theme: Existing autonomy and the targeting chain

insights.claim: Autonomy is long established in military systems: from Hammond's 1916 electric dog, the Norden bombsight, Vietnam-era precision-guided bombs, to the Patriot and CIWS in the 1980s that detect and fire faster than any human.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: New AI weapons are an evolution of decades-old capability.
insights.locator: What few people understand is how much autonomy

insights.claim: Military operations have three stages: the decision to start an operation, operational targeting, and use of specific weapons, and humans decide at each of the first two stages before any autonomous weapon is used.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Separates AI decision support from weapon autonomy when assessing regulation.
insights.locator: It is also important to distinguish the decision to deploy

insights.claim: CENTCOM has used the Maven Smart System during Operation Epic Fury to aggregate information streams into one dashboard, reportedly with LLMs as one of several inputs to speed targeting.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Shows LLM use in military targeting is at the decision-support layer.
insights.locator: For example, U.S. Central Command has used the Maven Smart System

insights.claim: Weapons can be classified by whether a machine selects targets, whether it engages them, and whether a human can supervise and halt it, yielding five types: unguided, semi-autonomous supervised or unsupervised, and autonomous supervised or unsupervised.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Provides a scheme to map any weapon system and its regulatory treatment.

insights.claim: Semi-autonomous weapons without supervision after launch have existed since the 1960s, including radar-guided missiles and AMRAAM, with Iran's Shahed-136 cited as a current example.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Much feared autonomy is old technology already fielded.
insights.locator: Semi-autonomous weapon systems with no human supervision after launch

insights.claim: CIWS, deployed since the early 1980s, has an automatic mode that selects and engages targets when too many for a human operator, and has been used to shoot down Houthi one-way attack drones.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Supervised autonomous defense is established practice for countering drone swarms.

insights.claim: Unsupervised autonomous weapons have no data link for humans to override and are what fully autonomous weapon usually means; Russia's Molniya-2 appears to be an example, and Ukraine's TFL-1 with last-mile autonomy blends categories.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Battlefield evidence of growing unsupervised autonomy in Ukraine and Russia.
insights.locator: Autonomous weapon systems without human supervision have no data link

insights.claim: A literal killer robots ban could affect CIWS, while a narrower ban sparing CIWS might miss concerning AI-enabled systems, and a mandatory datalink or override requirement could prohibit decades-old semi-autonomous weapons.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Poorly drafted rules could sweep in legacy systems or miss new ones; watch NDAA language.
insights.locator: Not All Military Autonomy Is Created Equal

insights.claim: The Senate's draft NDAA contains dozens of pages of micro-level regulation on Pentagon use of autonomous weapons and AI, reflecting misunderstanding driven by congressional AI concern.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Defense AI procurement rules may tighten; watch NDAA outcomes.
insights.locator: Misunderstanding around AI and weapon systems is already affecting policy

insights.claim: More autonomous weapons are likely inevitable because widespread electronic warfare and jamming force militaries to use systems that function without a data link, as Ukraine does with cheap drones with modest onboard vision software.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Supports demand for cheap autonomous drones and counter-jamming tech.
insights.locator: It is clear that communications will be contested in any war

insights.claim: LLMs add unclear operational value to edge-deployed weapons and would greatly expand testing and evaluation, and most worrying autonomous weapons run on far simpler software, so the weapons debate and the generative AI safety debate address different problems.
insights.speaker: Michael C. Horowitz
insights.so_what: Frontier-LLM exposure to weapons autonomy is limited; narrow vision models matter more.
insights.quote: the autonomous weapon system debate and the generative AI safety and alignment debate are about different problems
